questions.question: According to the course, what is the core algorithmic idea behind FlashAttention? [ref_2]
choices: Tiled GEMM + Online Softmax
Low-rank approximation of the attention matrix
Sparse attention with a fixed random sparsity pattern
Quantizing Q, K and V to FP8 before the softmax
questions.reference_answer: Tiled GEMM + Online Softmax. The course states the core algorithmic idea is "Tiled GEMM + Online Softmax" [ref_2].
scoring_points: Selects 'Tiled GEMM + Online Softmax'.
Recognizes that both components (tiling and online softmax) are required, not just one.
Does not confuse FlashAttention with an approximation or quantization technique.
knowledge_points: FlashAttention core idea (tiling + online softmax to avoid materializing the attention matrix)

questions.question: Why is naive attention slow, according to the course? [ref_1]
choices: It materializes the full score matrix S = QK^T and probability matrix P = softmax(S), causing high HBM traffic
It uses too few CUDA threads per block, so the GPU is under-occupied
It recomputes the softmax denominator once per output element
It cannot use Tensor Cores because the softmax is non-linear
questions.reference_answer: Naive attention "Materializes the full score matrix $S = QK^{T}$ and probability matrix $P = \text{softmax}(S)$", which leads to "High HBM traffic: write S, read S, write P, read P" [ref_1].
scoring_points: Selects the option about materializing S and P.
Identifies HBM traffic (writing/reading S and P) as the bottleneck.
Does not attribute the slowness to thread occupancy or Tensor Core limitations.
knowledge_points: FlashAttention core idea (tiling + online softmax to avoid materializing the attention matrix)

questions.question: In the course's description of FlashAttention, how are QK^T and PV computed? [ref_1]
choices: Block by block, instead of materializing the full N x N matrix
By first writing the full N x N score matrix to HBM and then reading it back
By approximating the softmax with a linear kernel
By computing only the diagonal blocks of the attention matrix
questions.reference_answer: FlashAttention uses tiled GEMM: "Compute QK^{T} and PV block by block instead of materializing the full N  $ \times $ N matrix." [ref_1]
scoring_points: Selects the block-by-block option.
States that the full N x N matrix is never materialized.
Does not claim the result is an approximation or that only diagonal blocks are used.
knowledge_points: FlashAttention core idea (tiling + online softmax to avoid materializing the attention matrix)

questions.question: Which statement about the numerical result of FlashAttention is correct according to the course? [ref_1]
choices: It computes exact attention, not an approximation
It is a low-rank approximation that trades accuracy for speed
It approximates the softmax by dropping small entries below a threshold
It is exact only when the sequence length is a multiple of the tile size
questions.reference_answer: The course lists "Exact attention, not approximation" among the reasons FlashAttention is faster [ref_1].
scoring_points: Selects 'exact attention, not an approximation'.
Recognizes that the speedup comes from IO/memory-traffic reduction, not from dropping computation.
Does not impose a tile-size divisibility condition on exactness.
knowledge_points: FlashAttention core idea (tiling + online softmax to avoid materializing the attention matrix)

questions.question: In the naive online softmax kernel, what does the update `d = d * expf(m - m_new) + expf(input[j] - m_new);` accomplish? [ref_8]
choices: It rescales the previously accumulated normalizer to the new running maximum and adds the new element's term
It resets the normalizer to zero whenever a new maximum is found
It computes the final softmax output for element j
It stores the running maximum m into shared memory for the next block
questions.reference_answer: Pass 1 is described as "// Pass 1: update running maximum m and running normalizer d together". The term `d * expf(m - m_new)` rescales the old accumulator from the old maximum m to the new maximum m_new, and `expf(input[j] - m_new)` adds the new element's contribution, so d stays a valid normalizer under the updated maximum [ref_8].
scoring_points: Identifies the rescaling of the old accumulator by exp(m - m_new).
Identifies the addition of the new element's term exp(x_j - m_new).
Explains that this keeps d consistent with the updated running maximum.
Does not claim d is reset to zero or that this line produces the final output.

questions.question: In the course's online softmax kernel, how many passes over the input vector are made, and what does each do? [ref_8]
choices: Two passes: pass 1 updates the running maximum m and normalizer d together; pass 2 computes the final softmax values in parallel
One pass: the running maximum, normalizer and output are all produced in a single loop
Three passes: one for the maximum, one for the sum, one for the division
Two passes: pass 1 computes the maximum, pass 2 computes the sum and the output
questions.reference_answer: The kernel has "// Pass 1: update running maximum m and running normalizer d together" followed by "// Pass 2: compute final Softmax values in parallel". The key saving is that the maximum and the normalizer are accumulated together in one scan, rather than in separate passes [ref_8].
scoring_points: States that there are two passes.
Describes pass 1 as jointly updating m and d.
Describes pass 2 as computing the final normalized outputs in parallel.
Contrasts this with the naive three-pass (max, sum, divide) approach.

questions.question: Why does stable softmax subtract the maximum m = max_j(x_j) before exponentiating? [ref_13]
choices: To prevent overflow, and to avoid catastrophic underflow by making max(x_j - c) = 0
To make the output distribution uniform across all classes
To reduce the number of floating-point multiplications in the denominator
Because exp(x_j - m) is a different function from exp(x_j) and changes the result
questions.reference_answer: The course states the requirement to prevent overflow and then: "To avoid catastrophic underflow: Choose $c$ s.t. $max(x_{j}-c)=0$", denoting the chosen c as m = max_j(x_j) [ref_13].
scoring_points: Mentions overflow prevention as one purpose.
Mentions avoiding catastrophic underflow / making the largest exponent zero.
Recognizes that subtracting a constant does not change the mathematical softmax result.
Does not claim it makes the distribution uniform.

questions.question: The course gives the example x = (1000, 1001, 1002) to motivate stable softmax. What problem does it illustrate? [ref_19]
choices: The sum of exp(x_j) may overflow, since exp(1000) is about 1.97e434 and exceeds max(float64) of about 1.8e308
The sum of exp(x_j) may underflow to zero because the values are too large
The softmax output is not a valid probability distribution for large inputs
The maximum operation is undefined when inputs exceed 1000
questions.reference_answer: The page states "problem:  $ \sum_{j=1}^{V} exp(x_{j}) $ may overflow example 1:" and shows exp(1000) ≈ 1.97e434 while max(float64) ≈ 1.8e308 < exp(1000) [ref_19].
scoring_points: Identifies overflow of the exponential sum as the problem.
Cites the concrete magnitudes (exp(1000) ≈ 1.97e434 vs max(float64) ≈ 1.8e308).
Does not misdescribe the failure as underflow or as an invalid distribution.

questions.question: In the shared-memory tiling GEMM kernel, why is `__syncthreads()` called after loading a tile and again after the compute loop? [ref_18]
choices: The first waits until the whole tile has been loaded into shared memory; the second ensures all threads finish using the tile before the next tile overwrites it
Both calls are only needed to synchronize the final write of C to global memory
The first synchronizes global memory writes; the second synchronizes the host and the device
They are optional performance hints that have no effect on correctness
questions.reference_answer: The code comments read "// Wait until the whole tile has been loaded" before the compute loop, and after it: "Make sure all threads finish using this tile before loading the next tile". Both barriers protect the shared-memory tiles from races between loading and computing [ref_18].
scoring_points: Explains the first barrier as waiting for the tile load to complete.
Explains the second barrier as preventing the next tile load from overwriting data still in use.
Identifies the hazard as a race on shared memory.
Does not describe the barriers as optional or as host/device synchronization.

questions.question: In the tiled GEMM kernel, what does the loop `for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++)` iterate over? [ref_18]
choices: The K dimension, moving tile by tile and accumulating into the thread's partial sum
The output rows of C, one row per iteration
The batch dimension of the input matrices
The number of thread blocks launched in the grid
questions.reference_answer: The comment above the loop is "// Move along the K dimension tile by tile", and inside it each thread loads one element of A and one of B into shared memory and accumulates `sum += As[ty][k] * Bs[k][tx];` [ref_18].
scoring_points: Identifies the loop as walking the K (reduction) dimension tile by tile.
Notes that each iteration loads a new A/B tile into shared memory and accumulates into sum.
Does not confuse it with iterating over output rows, batches, or blocks.

questions.question: Which formula does the course give for the attention operator, and how many GEMMs does it decompose into? [ref_7]
choices: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V, decomposed into 2 GEMMs (S = QK^T and O = PV) plus 1 softmax
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T) V, decomposed into 1 GEMM plus 1 softmax
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / d_k) V, decomposed into 3 GEMMs
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QV^T / sqrt(d_k)) K, decomposed into 2 GEMMs plus 1 softmax
questions.reference_answer: The course gives "$$ Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V $$" and labels the decomposition "2 GEMM" with S = QK^T (gemm 1) and O = PV (gemm 2), plus "1 Softmax" [ref_7].
scoring_points: Selects the formula with the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling and the V multiplication.
States that there are 2 GEMMs: S = QK^T and O = PV.
States that there is 1 softmax applied to the scaled scores.
Does not omit the sqrt(d_k) scaling or swap K and V.
